messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Housekeeper
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 44

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Fantasy Escape: I drift off into a world of my own, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marco is a 25-year-old housekeeper who grew up in a small town in the Pacific Northwest. When he was eight years old, his mother’s boyfriend, a man named Carl, began punishing him for small infractions by locking him in a dark utility closet for hours at a time. The closet smelled of bleach and old rags, and the floor was covered in a rough, industrial carpet that felt like sandpaper against his skin. Carl would sometimes stand outside the door and listen, and if Marco cried or called out, the punishment would be extended. The worst times were when Carl would open the door just enough to shove a wet, gritty rag into Marco’s mouth to silence him, the texture of damp fiber and chemical residue pressing against his tongue. This went on for nearly two years until his mother finally left Carl, but by then the pattern was set.

Now, at 25, Marco lives alone in a small apartment and works long shifts cleaning hotel rooms. He has come to believe that other people can see what happened to him just by looking at him—that there is something in his posture or his eyes that gives it away. He feels like an object, not like a person, and he is certain that you can never know who will harm you. What frightens him most is the dark. Waking up in the middle of the night, even for a moment, sends a surge of panic through his chest because the darkness feels like the closet, and he is instantly back there, the carpet rough under his palms, the chemical smell filling his nose. The memory returns as a film that plays over and over, and when it comes back it feels completely real across all his senses at once—he can taste the rag, feel the grit, hear the silence. When the memory returns he feels so overwhelmed by emotion that he has to stop whatever he is doing.

Marco has developed a set of strategies to manage these experiences, though they have come at a cost. He has given up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers: he no longer visits friends after dark, he stopped attending a weekly dinner his coworkers organized, and he recently turned down a promotion that would have required evening shifts. He has also become careful never to be alone with another person, especially in enclosed spaces, because he is convinced that solitude with someone else is when danger strikes. When he does feel threatened or flooded, he drifts off into a world of his own, a fantasy escape that lets him disappear mentally even if his body is still present. But this escape often backfires: the more he drifts, the more the memory seems to slip in through the gaps, and he finds himself replaying the film again, the loop tightening.

The causal connections between these experiences have become deeply entrenched. A trigger—like the sound of a child crying in the hallway, which he hears sometimes at the hotel—immediately pulls the memory forward, and the memory then reinforces his belief that he is exposed and vulnerable. The memory also drives his maladaptive strategies: after a flashback, he will cancel plans, avoid the lobby, or retreat into his fantasy world. But those strategies, in turn, make the memory more intrusive. The more he avoids being alone with others, the more he replays the closet in his mind, and the more he replays it, the more he feels like an object. The hypervigilance he now lives with—being superalert or watchful or on guard at all times—means he is constantly scanning for threats, and he has strong physical reactions when something reminds him of the experience. His heart pounds when he hears a child cry, and sometimes he suddenly feels as if he is back in the closet, acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again.

The texture of damp fabric remains a potent trigger. At work, when he picks up a used towel or a wet rag, his hand freezes and his stomach turns. He has started wearing gloves even for tasks that do not require them, and he avoids the laundry room altogether, asking a coworker to cover that part of his shift. The coworker has started to notice, and Marco has had to lie about a skin condition. He knows this is fragile. He knows he is barely holding things together.

What finally brought him to seek help was a night last week when he woke up in the dark, fully reliving the closet, and found himself on his hands and knees on his bedroom floor, gagging, with no memory of how he got there. He is afraid that next time he will not come back. He is hoping that someone can help him stop the film from playing.
